title: Six-week cough in a young woman
desc: This station involves a focused cough history and examination of Jenny Sok, a 26-year-old law student who was born in Cambodia and has had a worsening productive cough for 6 weeks. In Part 2 the candidate interprets her observations, blood results and chest X-ray, gives the most likely diagnosis, and plans investigation, urgent referral and safety netting in general practice.
focus: Chronic productive cough with haemoptysis: a structured cough history with differential clusters and risk factors, then recognising and starting the work-up of suspected pulmonary tuberculosis
stem: You are a medical student on your general practice rotation. Jenny Sok is a 26-year-old law student who has come to see her GP about a worsening cough. The GP has asked you to see her first.
tasks: Take a focused history from Jenny and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Jenny's observations, her blood results and her chest X-ray report. Give an ISBAR handover including your interpretation, state your most likely diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Jenny Sok, a 26-year-old law student. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. You are tired and fed up with the cough, which interrupts you while you talk, and you are a bit worried about the blood. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "I've just been having this cough for ages now…"

The cough (give only when asked):

  • Onset and course: started about 6 weeks ago. It came on gradually and has been there all the time since, getting steadily worse. You have never had a cough like this before.
  • Sputum: you cough up yellow-green phlegm, about a teaspoon at a time, several times a day.
  • Blood (only if asked about blood): for the last 5 days there have been bright red streaks of blood in the phlegm a few times a day. You have never coughed up pure blood or clots.
  • Pain: no pain with the cough and no chest pain at all.
  • Worse: in cold weather, especially in the mornings. Better: nothing helps, including the Codral.
  • Impact: "It's so distracting. I can't concentrate on study or work, and I can't enjoy anything." You have stopped going to badminton.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • Tiredness: exhausted for the past month or so.
  • Fever: you feel hot and a bit feverish on and off, mostly in the evenings. You have not measured it. No shaking chills.
  • Weight: you have lost about 5 kg over the last 2 months without trying (from 55 kg). Your jeans are loose.
  • Breathlessness: for a few weeks you get short of breath on stairs and could not keep up at badminton. Not breathless at rest.
  • No drenching night sweats. Your appetite is about the same as usual. No hoarse voice.
  • No wheeze, no hay fever, eczema or asthma, and no triggers such as dust or pets.
  • No breathlessness lying flat, no waking at night breathless, no ankle swelling.
  • No long flights or trips recently, no operations, no time stuck in bed, no calf pain or swelling, no sharp pain on breathing in.
  • No runny nose, sore throat or cold before the cough started.
  • No headache, neck stiffness, confusion, back pain or lumps in your neck.

Background (only if asked):

  • Born: in Cambodia; you came to Australia as a child. You go back every year to visit relatives. Your last trip was about 9 months ago, for 4 weeks over the summer break, staying with family.
  • Travel (if asked): no travel in the last 9 months; if asked about overseas travel, give the Cambodia trips above.
  • Contacts: No one around you has been sick. You do not know of anyone with tuberculosis.
  • Exposure: no dust, chemicals or animals at work or uni.
  • Immune system (if asked): no steroids or other medicines that lower immunity, no diabetes, never had an HIV test. No injecting drug use, no blood transfusions, one partner in the past year.

Past medical history: nil. No lung disease, no chest infections, no hospital admissions. Never treated for tuberculosis. Vaccinations are up to date. If asked about BCG: "I think I had one as a baby, there's a little scar on my arm."

Medications: the oral contraceptive pill daily; Codral Cold & Flu tablets from the chemist for the cough for the past 2 weeks; a multivitamin.

Allergies: none.

Family history: your dad died at 49 in Cambodia; you do not know what from. Your mum and brother are well.

Social history:

  • You smoke 10 cigarettes a day and have for 3 years. Alcohol 2 to 3 drinks on a weekend. No other drugs.
  • You live with your mum and your younger brother (22). Full-time law student with casual work in a clothing shop. Well supported by family and friends.
  • You go for an occasional run and play badminton (until recently). You eat mostly home-made meals.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you think it is a bad chest infection made worse by smoking. The blood scares you, and you have exams in 3 weeks. You hope for antibiotics or a stronger cough medicine so you can get back to study.

Question to raise (once, near the end of Part 1): "Is the blood something serious?" Settle if the candidate explains honestly that it needs tests today without either dismissing it or frightening you.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: thin young woman, alert, talking in full sentences with an occasional loose cough. Not in respiratory distress. Mildly pale. Not cyanosed. Sputum pot (if asked): yellow-green mucopurulent sputum with flecks of bright red blood.
  • Vital signs (10:20): temperature 37.8 °C; HR 92 beats/min regular; BP 112/70 mmHg; RR 18/min; SpO2 97% on room air. Weight 50 kg, height 160 cm (BMI 19.5).
  • Hands: no clubbing. Mild nicotine staining of the right index and middle fingers.
  • Lymph nodes: no cervical, supraclavicular or axillary lymphadenopathy.
  • Respiratory: trachea midline. Expansion slightly reduced at the right apex. Percussion resonant throughout. Coarse crackles over the right upper zone, anteriorly below the clavicle and posteriorly above the scapula. No bronchial breathing, no wheeze. The left lung and right base are clear.
  • Cardiovascular: JVP not raised. Heart sounds dual, no murmurs. No peripheral oedema.
  • Legs: calves soft, non-tender and equal in size.
  • Other: BCG scar on the left upper arm. Abdomen soft, no hepatosplenomegaly. No neck stiffness. No spinal tenderness.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self by name and role (medical student), confirms Jenny's identity and gains consent for the history and examination.
Empathic, non-judgemental approach (including about smoking), acknowledges how the cough is affecting her study and uses plain language.
History
Characterises the cough:

kids.x: Onset and duration: 6 weeks, gradual, constant and progressive, no previous episodes.
Productive of yellow-green sputum, with the amount; no associated pain.
Aggravating and relieving factors: worse in cold weather, nothing relieves it.

check.x: Asks specifically about haemoptysis and finds bright red streaks in the sputum for 5 days, with the amount (streaks only, no frank blood or clots).
Asks how the cough affects daily life: hard to work and study, cannot enjoy leisure, stopped badminton.
Asks about constitutional symptoms: fever, night sweats, fatigue, appetite, and weight loss quantified (5 kg in 2 months, unintentional), plus breathlessness.
check.d: Critical threshold: fever and quantified unintentional weight loss; the remaining symptoms are supporting.

check.x: Uses cluster questions to screen differentials and stratify risk:
check.d: Source marking: full marks for cluster questions covering at least 4 differentials with risk factor stratification. Credit sub-item 1 separately; it must be covered.

kids.x: Tuberculosis: immunosuppression (HIV, steroids, diabetes) and previous TB or TB treatment.
Pneumonia: acute onset, chest pain, rigors.
Lung cancer: anorexia, night sweats, hoarse voice, smoking.
Pulmonary embolism: immobility or long travel, pleuritic pain, calf pain or swelling, on the oral contraceptive pill.
Heart failure: orthopnoea, PND, ankle oedema.

check.x: Takes a travel and exposure history: born in Cambodia, travels there annually (last trip about 9 months ago), no recent travel, no sick or known TB contacts, no occupational exposure.
Takes a smoking history with pack-years (10 a day for 3 years, 1.5 pack-years) and asks about alcohol and other drugs.
Past medical history: no lung disease, infections, hospitalisations or previous TB treatment; vaccinations up to date, including BCG.
Medications (oral contraceptive pill, Codral Cold & Flu, multivitamin) and allergies (nil).
Family history: father died at 49 in Cambodia, cause unknown; asks about TB or lung disease in the family.
Social history: lives with her mother and brother, full-time law student with casual retail work, supports, exercise and diet.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations, including her worry about the blood and her exams.
Examination
Requests vital signs with temperature, SpO2 and weight, and notes the low-grade temperature (37.8 °C) and weight of 50 kg (BMI 19.5).
General inspection: body habitus or wasting, pallor, cyanosis, work of breathing; asks to inspect the sputum.
Examines the hands for clubbing and nicotine staining.
Palpates the cervical, supraclavicular and axillary lymph nodes.
Respiratory examination (trachea, expansion, percussion, auscultation front and back) and finds coarse crackles in the right upper zone.
Cardiovascular examination and both calves (JVP, heart sounds, oedema, calf swelling or tenderness).
Looks for a BCG scar and signs of spread outside the lungs (hepatosplenomegaly, neck stiffness, spinal tenderness).
Interpretation
Chest X-ray: confirms patient details, date, view (PA) and adequacy.
Chest X-ray: describes multifocal patchy right upper lobe opacification with no effusion and a clear left lung.
States that, with the history, the X-ray is most likely pulmonary tuberculosis, and that an X-ray cannot confirm it: microbiology is needed.

Gives at least two relevant differentials, each with a reason for and against: community-acquired pneumonia (against: 6-week course, weight loss, normal WCC); lung cancer (against: age 26, 1.5 pack-years, no mass or hilar enlargement); pulmonary embolism (the pill and haemoptysis, but an infective picture, no pleuritic pain, SpO2 97%); or melioidosis (Cambodian exposure; alert the lab).

Bloods: mild normocytic anaemia, raised platelets, CRP and ESR and low albumin fit chronic inflammation; normal white cell count; normal liver and kidney function as a baseline for TB treatment; β-hCG negative.
Observations: low-grade temperature (37.8 °C) but normal heart rate, breathing rate, blood pressure and SpO2, so she is not septic or hypoxic and can be managed as an outpatient with urgent referral.
Management
Infection control: surgical mask on Jenny, a separate room away from the waiting area, and P2/N95 respirators for staff.
check.d: Critical threshold: surgical mask on Jenny AND a separate room away from the waiting area, in either part; P2/N95 respirators for staff are supporting.

check.x: Orders three sputum specimens for AFB microscopy and mycobacterial culture.
Requests TB NAAT on at least one specimen, including an early-morning specimen.
Refers urgently to the state TB service or a respiratory physician by phone the same day; requests HIV (with consent), hepatitis B/C and HbA1c or leaves these to the TB service.
States TB is notifiable, and the state TB service or public health unit arranges contact tracing.
Does not start TB treatment in general practice, and avoids fluoroquinolones (they can mask TB and select resistance).
Safety netting
Explains the likely diagnosis in plain words (a treatable infection, curable with a full course of tablets), addresses her worry about the blood and her exams, and checks her understanding.

Advises her to stay home (no uni, work, public transport or visitors) until the TB service says she is not infectious; she travels home by private car wearing a surgical mask, and the TB service will advise on transport to the clinic.
check.d: Critical threshold: tells her to stay home from uni, work and public transport (or to avoid other people outside the household) until the TB service says she is not infectious. Travelling home by private car in a mask, no visitors and transport to the clinic are supporting.

check.x: Explains her mother, brother and close contacts will be offered screening and should see a doctor if they develop cough, fever or weight loss.

Red flags in plain words: call 000 for coughing up more than streaks of blood (for example a few spoonfuls or more) or severe breathlessness; go to ED for chest pain, high fever, feeling faint, or a severe headache, stiff neck or confusion.
check.d: Critical threshold: must name frank haemoptysis (more than streaks) and severe breathlessness as reasons to call 000, plus at least one ED trigger.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: TB clinic within days, GP review of the sputum results, and who to call if the TB service has not contacted her.

part2.lead: Jenny had a chest X-ray and blood tests at the imaging and collection centre next door at lunchtime and has come back this afternoon. She is waiting to see you again. Here are her observations, her blood results and her chest X-ray report.
part2.patient:
Jenny is present for question 4 only. When the candidate explains the plan, she asks once, if not already covered: "I've got exams in 3 weeks and a shift on Saturday. Can I still go?"

She is upset about missing uni and work but accepts it once she hears why staying home matters and that the treatment works. If the candidate uses jargon ("AFB", "notifiable") without explaining it, she asks what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Taken in the practice on room air. Weight 50 kg today (55 kg two months ago, by her report).
handover.model:
Read: at 10:20 temperature 37.8 °C (low-grade, below the 38 °C fever threshold and in the normal chart zone, but fitting her evening fevers; the paracetamol in Codral may be masking higher peaks); HR 92, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air and BP 112/70 are within normal adult ranges. The 15:50 set is almost the same. Weight 50 kg, a loss of about 9% in 2 months.

For Jenny: a chronic illness with systemic features (fever, weight loss), but she is not septic, not hypoxic and haemodynamically stable. Nothing here needs emergency transfer.

What it changes: she can be managed as an outpatient with an urgent referral to the TB service. She would need ED if she became hypoxic, hypotensive or tachycardic, or coughed up a large amount of blood.

rows.note: Repeat set on return from imaging

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected 12:40 at the collection centre. No haemolysis.
handover.model:
Read: Hb 112 g/L with a normal MCV (mild normocytic anaemia), platelets 438 (mildly raised), normal white cell count and differential. CRP 38 and ESR 46 are raised, albumin 33 is low. Electrolytes, creatinine and liver function are normal. Serum β-hCG is negative.

For Jenny: a picture of chronic inflammation (most likely anaemia of chronic disease; iron deficiency is not excluded), with reactive thrombocytosis and low albumin, which fits a 6-week infection with weight loss such as TB. Iron studies would help. A normal white cell count makes acute bacterial pneumonia less likely, but none of these tests can confirm or exclude TB.

What it changes: the normal liver and kidney function are the baseline before TB drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide can damage the liver). The negative pregnancy test matters for contraception advice, any CT, and planning around pregnancy during treatment.

labs.title: Urea, electrolytes and creatinine; liver function tests

handover.label: Chest X-ray report
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, PA view, taken at 12:20 today.

Patient: Jenny Sok, 26-year-old woman.

Clinical details: 6-week progressive productive cough, blood-streaked sputum for 5 days, low-grade fever, 5 kg weight loss. Born in Cambodia, travels there annually. Smoker. Crackles right upper zone.

Comparison: no previous chest imaging.

Technique: adequate inspiration, not rotated, adequate exposure.

Findings:

  • Lungs: multifocal patchy airspace opacification in the right upper lobe. No definite cavitation on this view. The left lung and the right middle and lower zones are clear. No mass seen.
  • Hila and mediastinum: hila of normal size and position; no hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Trachea central.
  • Pleura: no pleural effusion, no pneumothorax.
  • Heart: normal size and outline.
  • Bones and soft tissues: unremarkable.

Conclusion: multifocal patchy opacification in the right upper lobe. In this clinical context, pulmonary tuberculosis is the leading consideration; infective consolidation from another cause is the differential. Sputum for AFB microscopy, mycobacterial culture and TB nucleic acid amplification is recommended. CT chest may help if the diagnosis remains uncertain.
handover.model:
Read: Jenny Sok, 26, PA chest X-ray today, adequate film. Multifocal patchy opacification in the right upper lobe with no definite cavity, no hilar lymphadenopathy, no effusion and a clear left lung. Heart and bones normal.

For Jenny: upper lobe disease with a 6-week progressive productive cough, haemoptysis, fever, weight loss and regular travel to Cambodia, where TB is common, makes pulmonary tuberculosis the most likely diagnosis. Bacterial pneumonia is the main alternative. No mass or hilar lymphadenopathy, which argues against lung cancer. An X-ray suggests TB but cannot confirm it.

What it changes: treat her as possibly infectious now: mask and separate room, three sputum specimens for AFB microscopy, culture and NAAT, urgent referral to the TB service, and no fluoroquinolones.

ask: You are now calling the registrar at the TB clinic of the local hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Jenny, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Jenny now, here in general practice.
Jenny has come back in. Explain the plan to her, then tell me what follow-up you would arrange.
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student with the GP at the practice. Jenny Sok, 26.
  • Situation: 6-week progressive productive cough, blood-streaked sputum for 5 days, fever, 5 kg weight loss. Suspected pulmonary TB, requesting urgent review.
  • Background: born in Cambodia, visits every year (last trip 9 months ago). Smokes 1.5 pack-years. No past history. Takes the OCP. Lives with her mother and brother. Law student and retail worker.
  • Assessment: T 37.8 °C, other observations normal, SpO2 97% on room air. Weight 50 kg. Right upper zone crackles. Bloods: Hb 112, platelets 438, CRP 38, ESR 46 and albumin 33 (chronic inflammation), WCC normal, LFTs and renal function normal, β-hCG negative. CXR: multifocal patchy right upper lobe opacification, probably TB.
  • Recommendation: TB clinic review within days. Sputum ×3 for AFB, culture and NAAT ordered. I have masked her and moved her to a separate room, and I have advised her to isolate at home. Please advise on notification and contact tracing.

Most likely: pulmonary tuberculosis. For it: a 6-week progressive productive cough with recent haemoptysis, low-grade fever, fatigue, breathlessness, 5 kg unintentional weight loss, born in and travelling yearly to Cambodia (high TB rates), right upper zone crackles, upper lobe opacification on CXR, chronic inflammatory bloods.

  • Community-acquired pneumonia: productive cough, fever, consolidation. Against: 6-week course, weight loss, normal WCC.
  • Lung cancer: smoker with haemoptysis and weight loss. Against: aged 26, only 1.5 pack-years, short history, no mass.
  • Pulmonary embolism: on the OCP, haemoptysis, breathlessness. Against: productive cough with fever, no pleuritic pain, normal calves, SpO2 97%.
  • Melioidosis: Cambodian exposure, upper lobe infiltrates, fever, weight loss. Against: no diabetes, heavy alcohol use or kidney disease; alert the lab to Burkholderia on sputum culture.
  • Bronchitis or bronchiectasis: against: no preceding cold, course too long; no recurrent infections or family history such as CF.

1. Infection control now: surgical mask for Jenny, separate room, P2/N95 respirators for staff.
  2. Sputum ×3 (at least one early morning) for AFB microscopy and culture, with TB NAAT on at least one specimen.
  3. Urgent referral to the state TB service or a respiratory physician by phone the same day, with a letter. HIV test with consent, hepatitis B and C serology and HbA1c, or leave these to the TB service.
  4. Notification: TB is notifiable; the state TB service or public health unit arranges contact tracing.
  5. No empirical TB treatment in general practice. No fluoroquinolones.
  6. Admit if she becomes hypoxic, coughs up a large amount of blood or cannot isolate.

• In plain words: probably TB, a lung infection that is curable with a full course of tablets. The tests will confirm it.
  • Isolation: stay home. No uni, work, public transport or visitors until the TB service says she is not infectious. Travel home today by private car wearing a surgical mask; the TB service will advise on transport to the clinic. Wear a mask around her family and cover her coughs. Her mother, brother and other close contacts will be offered screening and should see a doctor if they develop cough, fever or weight loss.
  • Red flags: call 000 for more than streaks of blood or severe breathlessness. Go to ED for chest pain, high fever, feeling faint, or a severe headache, stiff neck or confusion.
  • Follow-up: TB clinic within days, GP review of the sputum results, and call the practice if the TB service has not contacted her. Help with her exams (medical certificate, special consideration). Written information.

ddx.for: Six-week progressive productive cough with 5 days of haemoptysis, low-grade fever, fatigue, breathlessness and 5 kg weight loss; born in and travels annually to Cambodia; right upper zone crackles and right upper lobe opacification.
ddx.against: No known TB contact and no cavity seen on the plain film.

ddx.for: Productive yellow-green sputum, fever, right upper zone crackles and airspace opacification on the X-ray.
ddx.against: A 6-week gradual course with weight loss, no chest pain or rigors, and a normal white cell count.

ddx.for: Smoker with haemoptysis, weight loss and fatigue.
ddx.against: Aged 26 with only 1.5 pack-years and a 6-week history, no clubbing or lymphadenopathy, and no mass or hilar enlargement on the X-ray.

ddx.for: Takes the oral contraceptive pill and has haemoptysis and exertional breathlessness.
ddx.against: Gradual productive cough with fever, no pleuritic pain, no immobility or calf signs, SpO2 97% and a normal heart rate.

ddx.for: Cambodian exposure, chronic cough with upper lobe infiltrates, fever and weight loss.
ddx.against: No diabetes, heavy alcohol use or kidney disease; sputum culture with the lab alerted to Burkholderia will help exclude it.

ddx.for: Chronic productive cough with haemoptysis in a smoker, worse in cold weather.
ddx.against: No preceding coryza, 6 weeks of progressive symptoms with weight loss, and no previous chest infections, family history such as cystic fibrosis or clubbing.

guide:
Part 1 is set at about 10:20. The examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Item 9 follows the source marking: full credit needs cluster questions for at least four differentials with their risk factors, and the TB cluster (sub-item 1) must be covered. Credit item 33 if the candidate masks Jenny and moves her to a separate room at any point, including in Part 1.

Part 2 is set at about 16:00 the same day. If the candidate masked or isolated Jenny in Part 1, tell them she has been kept masked in the treatment room. Otherwise tell them she is unmasked in the main waiting room, and credit item 33 only if they now mask her and move her to a separate room. Hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. The actor is present for question 4 only: the candidate explains the plan to Jenny, and she asks her one question if the candidate has not covered it; the candidate then tells the examiner the follow-up. Credit X-ray interpretation (items 26 to 28) whether it is given in the ISBAR or in the diagnosis answer. If the candidate does not cover notification or contact tracing, do not prompt; leave those items unmarked.

A high-performing candidate characterises the cough and asks directly about blood. They quantify the weight loss, screen the differentials in clusters, and draw out the Cambodian birth and travel history and her household. In Part 2 they read the X-ray systematically, call it probable pulmonary TB and order three sputum specimens. They put her in a mask, refer urgently to the TB service, avoid fluoroquinolones, ask her to isolate at home and give specific red flags.

A borderline candidate takes a generic cough history without asking about haemoptysis, travel or weight. They may treat this as pneumonia with an antibiotic (especially a fluoroquinolone) and a review in a week, or say nothing about infection control, isolation or her contacts.
explain:
Diagnosis: suspected pulmonary tuberculosis

Jenny has a cough lasting more than 3 weeks with recent haemoptysis, low-grade fever, fatigue, breathlessness and 5 kg of unintentional weight loss. She was born in Cambodia, a country with high TB rates, and visits every year. A chronic cough with haemoptysis and weight loss in someone with time in an endemic country is TB until proven otherwise. Upper lobe disease on the chest X-ray fits post-primary (reactivation) TB. Other risk factors to stratify are known contact with TB, previous TB, HIV or other immunosuppression (steroids, biologics), diabetes, smoking, alcohol, homelessness and incarceration. Smoking raises both the risk of TB and the risk of a poor outcome.

Structuring the cough history

Ask how long the cough has lasted, whether it is productive and what the sputum looks like, whether there is blood and how much, the timing, triggers and relievers, and the effect on daily life (a good guide to severity). Then screen associated features in clusters for each differential, with the relevant positives and negatives:

  • TB: fever, night sweats, weight loss, contacts, travel or birth in an endemic country, immunosuppression.
  • Pneumonia: acute onset, fever, rigors, pleuritic chest pain.
  • Lung cancer: smoking, weight loss, anorexia, hoarseness, haemoptysis.
  • Pulmonary embolism: immobility, oestrogen, pleuritic pain, calf swelling.
  • Asthma: wheeze, atopy, triggers.
  • Heart failure: orthopnoea, PND, oedema.

Differentials

  • Pneumonia explains the productive cough and fever, but not 6 weeks of steady progression with weight loss and a normal white cell count.
  • Lung cancer must be kept in mind with haemoptysis in a smoker, but it is unlikely at 26 with 1.5 pack-years and a short history.
  • Acute bronchitis usually follows coryza and settles within about 3 weeks.
  • Bronchiectasis would usually have a history of recurrent infections or an underlying cause such as cystic fibrosis.
  • Pulmonary embolism is worth excluding because she takes the oral contraceptive pill and has haemoptysis, but her picture is infective.
  • Melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei) is endemic in Cambodia and northern Australia, can stay latent for years and causes upper lobe infiltrates that mimic TB, mainly in people with diabetes, heavy alcohol use or kidney disease, so alert the lab when sending sputum culture; paragonimiasis (lung fluke, from raw freshwater crab or crayfish) is a rarer cause of haemoptysis after time in South-East Asia.

Interpreting the results

  • Chest X-ray: start with the patient details, date, view and adequacy, then describe the findings structure by structure. Multifocal patchy right upper lobe opacification with this history is most likely pulmonary TB. Look also for cavitation (high bacillary load), hilar lymphadenopathy, effusion and miliary nodules. An X-ray suggests TB but does not prove it, and a normal film does not exclude it in an immunosuppressed patient.
  • Bloods: normocytic anaemia, thrombocytosis, raised CRP and ESR and low albumin reflect chronic inflammation; in a young woman who menstruates, iron studies help separate this from iron deficiency. Normal liver and kidney function are the baseline before treatment.
  • Observations: low-grade fever with otherwise normal values. She is stable for urgent outpatient care.

Management in general practice

  • Infection control first: a surgical mask for the patient, a separate room away from the waiting area, and P2/N95 respirators for staff (airborne precautions).
  • Microbiology: three sputum specimens, including an early-morning one, for AFB microscopy, mycobacterial culture with susceptibility testing and TB nucleic acid amplification (which also detects rifampicin resistance). Collect them outdoors or in a well-ventilated space. If she cannot produce sputum, the TB service may arrange induced sputum or bronchoscopy. An interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test does not diagnose active TB.
  • Referral and notification: refer urgently to the state TB service or a respiratory physician. TB is notifiable, and the state TB service or public health unit arranges contact tracing of household and other close contacts. Assessment and treatment through state TB services are free.
  • Avoid empirical antibiotics that mask TB: eTG advises against fluoroquinolones when TB is suspected, because they partly treat TB, delay the diagnosis and select for resistance. TB treatment is started by the TB service, not in general practice.
  • Associated testing: HIV testing with consent for everyone with TB, plus hepatitis B and C serology and diabetes screening.
  • Treatment (eTG, under the TB service): for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB, isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampicin for 4 months. Pyridoxine is usually given with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy, and treatment is often directly observed. Monitor liver function (hepatotoxicity) and vision and colour vision (ethambutol). Warn that rifampicin turns urine and tears orange.
  • Drug interactions: rifampicin induces liver enzymes and makes combined oral contraceptives unreliable, so another method is needed during treatment and for 4 weeks after stopping. Stop over-the-counter cold and flu tablets: they do not help a chronic cough, and the paracetamol in them can mask a fever.
  • Smoking: offer smoking cessation support, with a referral to Quitline and nicotine replacement therapy.
  • Isolation: she stays home from university, work and public transport until the TB service says she is no longer infectious.

Extrapulmonary spread

TB can spread beyond the lungs to the lymph nodes, pleura, spine, kidneys and meninges. TB meningitis is the most dangerous. Look for these sites if the presentation is more serious, and teach her to seek urgent care for headache, neck stiffness or confusion.

Safety netting

Call 000 for coughing up more than streaks of blood or for severe breathlessness. Go to ED for chest pain, high fever, faintness, or severe headache, stiff neck or confusion. Arrange the TB clinic appointment within days and a GP review when the sputum smear and NAAT results are back (usually within a few days of the last specimen; culture takes weeks). Make sure the patient knows whom to call if the clinic has not contacted her. Household members with a cough, fever or weight loss should see a doctor.
points: A cough lasting more than 3 weeks with haemoptysis, fever and weight loss in someone born in or travelling to a country with high TB rates is pulmonary TB until proven otherwise.
Structure the associated features in clusters for each differential (TB, pneumonia, lung cancer, PE, asthma, heart failure), and ask how the cough affects daily life to judge severity.
Read a chest X-ray systematically, starting with the patient details and view. Upper lobe opacification suggests TB, but only sputum AFB microscopy, culture and NAAT (three specimens) confirm it.
Suspected TB means a mask and a separate room now, urgent referral to the state TB service, notification and contact tracing, and isolation at home. Never use a fluoroquinolone empirically.

Standard treatment for drug-susceptible TB is 2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, then 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin. Rifampicin makes hormonal contraception unreliable.
TB can spread outside the lungs: headache, neck stiffness or confusion may mean TB meningitis and need emergency care.
